children: Circle has published a seven-part framework for judging whether wrapped assets are fit for institutional use. The test covers custody, reserves, redemption, compliance, operational resilience, governance and composability.

The core idea is a weakest-link rule. Circle's position is that a wrapped asset is only as strong as its worst-performing category, so a token with spotless custody and sloppy redemption still fails the test.
A wrapped asset is a token on one blockchain that represents an asset held somewhere else.
Circle's framework turns that into a checklist with seven categories:
Custody: who holds the underlying asset, and under what legal structure.
Reserves: whether the backing actually exists in full, and whether anyone can verify it.
Redemption: how holders convert the token back into the original asset.
Compliance: which regulator oversees the issuer and what rules apply.
Operational resilience: how well the system holds up when something breaks.
Governance: who makes decisions about the asset and how.
Composability: how easily the token plugs into other onchain applications and workflows.
Circle did not stop at theory. The same post runs its own product, cirBTC, or Circle Wrapped Bitcoin, through the seven-part test.
On compliance, cirBTC is issued through an affiliate regulated by the Bermuda Monetary Authority.
On custody, the underlying Bitcoin is held by Circle National Trust, which Circle describes as a federally chartered national trust bank.
On reserves, cirBTC is backed 1:1 by native BTC. Verification runs through Chainlink's Proof of Reserve system, which provides onchain confirmation of the reserves.

On redemption, cirBTC can be converted back through eligible workflows via Circle Mint. The word "eligible" matters: redemption runs through defined channels rather than being open to every holder on every platform.
The framework did not arrive in isolation. Circle has published a run of related pieces between August 18 and September 15, 2026, covering topics such as reserve transparency and risk controls.
Circle's broader aim, as outlined in the post, is to position cirBTC as a transparent and neutral collateral option for institutional workflows.
By publishing evaluation criteria, Circle is trying to define what "institutional grade" means for wrapped assets. Competing issuers may now face questions organized around Circle's seven categories.

For institutions, the framework offers a practical due diligence template. Treasury desks, lenders and trading firms weighing wrapped Bitcoin as collateral can use the seven dimensions to compare products side by side.

Redemption mechanics deserve close attention. Routing conversions through eligible Circle Mint workflows offers control, but it also defines who gets direct access to the underlying Bitcoin and who does not.

The composability category may prove the hardest to satisfy. A collateral asset is only useful if lending platforms, exchanges and settlement systems actually integrate it, and that depends on decisions made well outside Circle's control.

title: Circle outlines seven-part framework for evaluating institutional wrapped assets
